title: The cache that never hit
scenario: A shop's support bot runs on Claude Sonnet 5.5. Every request sends the same 6,000-token policy manual. The team turned on prompt caching to cut the bill, but the bill went up a little. You review the request layout and the usage numbers (exhibit).
exhibit:
REQUEST LAYOUT (same for every user)
system[0]  Today is 2026-10-06 09:14:07 UTC.   ~15 tokens
system[1]  refund and shipping policy manual   ~6,000 tokens
messages   the user's question                 ~40 tokens
cache_control: on the last block (the user's question)

USAGE (three requests, 2 minutes apart)
req  cache_creation_input_tokens  cache_read_input_tokens
1    6,055                        0
2    6,061                        0
3    6,048                        0

PRICES (Claude Sonnet 5.5, per million tokens)
base input $2   5m cache write $2.50   cache read $0.20

questions.prompt: Why is nothing ever read from the cache?

options.text: 6,000 tokens is below the minimum cacheable length for this model.
options.explanation: The Claude docs give 512 tokens as the minimum for Claude Sonnet 5.5. The usage also shows writes happening, which means the length is enough.

options.text: The requests are too far apart, so each entry expires first.
options.explanation: They are 2 minutes apart, inside the 5-minute default lifetime. Expiry is not the cause.

options.text: Prompt caching on Claude needs a beta header that is missing.
options.explanation: Caching works without a beta header here: the usage shows cache writes on every request.

options.text: The first block and the marked block change on every request.
options.explanation: Right. Cache hits need an identical prefix. The timestamp at the top changes each time, and the breakpoint sits on the changing question.

options.text: Remove the timestamp, and keep `cache_control` on the user's question.
options.explanation: Writes only happen at the breakpoint. With the mark on the question, which changes every time, no earlier entry is ever written to read back.

options.text: Put the manual first, the time after it, and `cache_control` on the manual.
options.explanation: Right. The Claude docs: mark the last block that stays the same across requests, and keep changing content after it.

options.text: Move `cache_control` to the timestamp block at the top.
options.explanation: The timestamp changes every request, so a breakpoint there writes a new entry each time and never gets a read.

options.text: Switch to the 1-hour cache so entries live longer.
options.explanation: A longer lifetime does not help when the prefix never matches. It would also make every write cost 2 times base instead of 1.25.

questions.prompt: After the fix, 10 requests arrive within 5 minutes. What does sending the manual cost, compared with one uncached pass of it?

options.text: About 2.15 times, against 10 times without caching.
options.explanation: Right. One write at 1.25 ($2.50 / $2) plus nine reads at 0.1 ($0.20 / $2) is 2.15.

options.text: About 1.25 times, because only the write is billed.
options.explanation: Reads are cheap but not free. Each of the nine reads costs 0.1 times the base price.

options.text: About 1 time, because cache reads are free.
options.explanation: The price list shows cache reads at $0.20 per million tokens, not zero.

options.text: About 12.5 times, because every request pays the write price.
options.explanation: Only the first request writes. The next nine read the stored prefix at 0.1 times base.

questions.prompt: At night, a request comes only every 20 minutes. What does the Claude documentation suggest?

options.text: Nothing changes, because the cache lasts 24 hours by default.
options.explanation: On Claude, the default lifetime is 5 minutes. A 24-hour retention option exists on some OpenAI models, not on Claude.

options.text: Keep the 5-minute cache; each read refreshes it, so it stays alive.
options.explanation: A read does refresh it, but only if it comes within 5 minutes. With 20-minute gaps, each entry expires first.

options.text: Use the 1-hour cache, which costs 2 times base to write.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic offers a 1-hour cache for when 5 minutes is too short, at 2 times the base input price for writes.

options.text: Turn caching off at night, since it never helps when traffic is low.
options.explanation: It can still help with the 1-hour lifetime, which spans the 20-minute gaps.
